result: The manuscript presents established knowledge about skeletal muscle anatomy and physiology, stating that skeletal muscles constitute approximately 60% of body mass, are responsible for movement and posture, regulate metabolism, and can undergo hypertrophy in response to exercise.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 represent well-established anatomical and physiological facts about skeletal muscle that are widely accepted in the scientific literature. These are appropriately presented as background knowledge without requiring experimental validation in this study.

result: The manuscript describes the established classification of muscle fiber types based on metabolic and contractile properties, including slow-twitch (oxidative, fatigue-resistant, MyHC 1) and fast-twitch (glycolytic, rapid-fatiguing, MyHC 2X/2B/2A) muscles, with type 2A fibers showing intermediate oxidative capacity.
evaluation: Claims C5-C20 present well-established muscle fiber type classifications supported by appropriate citations (Lieber 2010; Schiaffino and Reggiani 2011; Eggers et al. 2021; Murgia et al. 2021). These are foundational concepts appropriately used as background for the study.

result: Extraocular muscles (EOMs) are described as specialized muscles with different embryonic origin, atypical fiber types, unique properties (fastest contracting yet fatigue-resistant, high mitochondrial content, multiple MyHC isoforms), and differential disease susceptibility (spared in DMD but affected in recessive RYR1 myopathies).
evaluation: Claims C21-C27 are well-supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Porter et al. 1995; Fischer et al. 2002; Amburgey et al. 2013). These establish important background for understanding why EOMs were included in the proteomic analysis.

result: The manuscript describes congenital myopathies as genetically heterogeneous diseases affecting >20 genes, with RYR1 mutations being most common (~30% of cases). Recessive RYR1 mutations cause more severe disease with early onset, widespread muscle weakness including facial and EOM involvement, and reduced RyR1 protein content.
evaluation: Claims C28-C37 are appropriately supported by citations to published literature (Jungbluth et al. 2018; Amburgey et al. 2013; Lawal et al. 2018; Zhou et al. 2007; Monnier et al. 2008). C37 appropriately presents a hypothesis about mechanism. This provides essential clinical context for the study.

result: The dHT mouse model carries compound heterozygous RyR1 mutations (p.Q1970fsX16 causing nonsense-mediated decay and p.A4329D missense) and recapitulates human disease phenotypes including reduced RyR1 content, cores, myofibrillar disarray, DHPR misalignment, impaired EOM function, decreased mitochondria, and loss of EOM-specific MyHC.
evaluation: Claims C38-C46 are supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Elbaz et al. 2019; Eckhardt et al. 2020), establishing the validity of the mouse model used in this study. This is appropriate referencing of prior characterization work.

result: Proteomic comparison of WT EDL versus soleus muscles revealed >1800 differentially expressed proteins (q<0.05), with 1319 higher and 547 lower in soleus. Pathway analysis showed soleus enrichment in mitochondrial/oxidative metabolism proteins, while EDL was enriched in glycolysis, muscle contraction, and extracellular matrix proteins.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are directly supported by the proteomic data presented in Figure 2A-C. The findings align with established muscle fiber type differences and validate the proteomic approach. Statistical thresholds (q<0.05) are appropriate.

result: Proteomic comparison of WT EOM versus EDL revealed >2500 differentially expressed proteins (q<0.05), with 2074 higher and 508 lower in EOM. EOMs showed lower adaptive immunity/MHC class I proteins but higher mitochondrial/oxidative metabolism proteins compared to EDL, consistent with their continuous contractile activity.
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 are supported by proteomic data in Figure 2D-F and appropriate citations (Porter et al. 1995; Fischer et al. 2002). The interpretation linking high mitochondrial content to continuous eye movements is reasonable and well-supported.

result: Proteomic comparison of WT EOM versus soleus revealed >2000 differentially expressed proteins (q<0.05), with 1663 higher and 521 lower in EOM compared to soleus.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are directly supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 2H. The statistical threshold (q<0.05) is appropriate for multiple testing correction.

result: Detailed proteomic analysis of contractile and ECC proteins showed expected fiber-type differences: soleus enriched 32-197-fold in slow troponins and MyHC-1, while EDL enriched in α-actinin 3/4, myomesin 1, and ECC proteins (RyR1, DHPR complex, Stac3, junctophilin-1, triadin >50% higher), consistent with larger sarcotubular membrane volume in fast-twitch muscle.
evaluation: Claims C64-C73 are supported by proteomic data (Supplementary file 1a) and appropriate citations (Treves et al. 2009; Brillantes et al. 1994; Luff and Atwood 1971). The findings validate known muscle fiber type differences and confirm the reliability of the proteomic approach.

result: EOMs showed unique protein expression patterns including high MyHC-EO (29-fold vs EDL, 20-fold vs soleus), embryonic MyHC (49-fold vs soleus), cardiac isoforms, enrichment in SERCA2/calsequestrin 2, but reduced RyR1/DHPR/Stac3/junctophilin-1 compared to EDL, and enrichment in Stim1 and junctin/junctate compared to both EDL and soleus.
evaluation: Claims C74-C83 are supported by proteomic data (Supplementary files 1b-c). The findings validate known EOM specializations and reveal novel quantitative differences in ECC protein composition, providing important baseline data for understanding disease effects.

result: EDL muscles were enriched in parvalbumin and CaMKII α/γ, while soleus and EOMs were enriched in S100A1. More than 10 heat shock proteins were more abundant in soleus and EOMs versus EDL, including Hspb6 (16-fold higher in soleus) and Hspa12a (7-fold higher in EOM). Mitsugumin 53 was 2.8-fold higher in soleus. These proteins may protect type 1 fibers from damage in RYR1 mutations.
evaluation: Claims C84-C95 are supported by proteomic data and appropriate citations (Dreiza et al. 2010; Jungbluth et al. 2005; Lawal et al. 2018; Maglara et al. 2003; Martin et al. 1997; Cai et al. 2009). C95 appropriately presents a speculative hypothesis based on the data. This provides important mechanistic insights.

result: In dHT EDL muscles, 848 proteins were significantly misregulated (q<0.05): 529 upregulated and 319 downregulated. Pathway analysis revealed downregulation of extracellular matrix proteins including collagen assembly/degradation, ECM organization, and integrin interactions in dHT versus WT.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are supported by proteomic data in Figure 3A-B and pathway analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The statistical threshold is appropriate. The ECM findings represent a novel and important disease mechanism.

result: In dHT soleus muscles, 509 proteins were significantly misregulated (q<0.05): 339 upregulated and 170 downregulated. The overall number of protein changes was smaller in soleus than EDL, suggesting differential disease severity.
evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by proteomic data in Figure 3C-D. The comparison between muscle types is valid and supports the clinical observation that slow-twitch muscles are less affected in RYR1 myopathies.

result: In dHT EOMs, 677 proteins were significantly misregulated (q<0.05): 560 upregulated and 117 downregulated. Pathway analysis showed upregulation of citric acid cycle, electron transport chain, ATP synthesis, and uncoupling proteins involved in heat formation.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by clinical literature (Lawal et al. 2018; Amburgey et al. 2013; Jungbluth et al. 2018) and proteomic data (Figure 3E-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The metabolic upregulation may represent a compensatory response.

result: RyR1 was the only protein decreased across all three muscle types in dHT mice. Conversely, 39 proteins including Kelch-like protein 41, calmodulin kinase 2δ, aspartyl-β-hydroxylase, and ribosomal proteins (40S/60S subunits) were increased in all three muscle types.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by proteomic data in Figure 4A and D. The universal RyR1 decrease validates the mouse model, while the shared upregulated proteins suggest common adaptive responses across muscle types.

result: In dHT EDL muscles, ECC proteins were downregulated (RyR1 60%, FKBP12 36%, DHPRα1 23%, junctophilin-1 40%), while Asph increased 2-fold and SRP-35 increased 1.34-fold. Fast MyHC isoforms (2X, 2B) and α-actinin 3 decreased along with collagens. Heat shock proteins, ribosomal proteins, and CaMKII isoforms (1, 2α, 2β, 2δ) increased.
evaluation: Claims C110-C117 are supported by proteomic data in Table 1 and appropriate citations (Treves et al. 2000; Schiaffino and Reggiani 2011). The coordinated changes in ECC proteins, fiber type markers, ECM, and stress response proteins reveal complex disease mechanisms.

result: In dHT soleus muscles, ECC proteins (RyR1, DHPRα1s, junctophilin-1, triadin) decreased while junctin/junctate/β-hydroxylase and SERCA2 increased. Troponin 3 decreased 30%. CaMKII IIδ/γ and S100A1 increased. Ribosomal proteins (40S/60S) increased.
evaluation: Claims C118-C123, C125 are supported by proteomic data in Table 2 and appropriate citations (Treves et al. 1997; Prosser et al. 2011). The pattern differs from EDL, suggesting muscle-type-specific disease responses.

result: Ribosomal protein content (40S/60S subunits) significantly increased in all three dHT muscle types. In normal muscle, ribosomal proteins increase with hypertrophy/training but decrease with age. The authors interpret this as an adaptive response to preserve protein compartment integrity and increase protein turnover.
evaluation: Claims C126-C129 are supported by proteomic data and appropriate citation (Ubadia-Mohien et al. 2019). C129 presents a reasonable interpretation of the data as an adaptive response, though the functional consequences require further validation.

result: Kelch-like protein 41 (KLH41), which is mutated in nemaline myopathy and regulates muscle protein homeostasis through interaction with MuRF1, is upregulated in all three dHT muscle types and may be activated in response to muscle damage for adaptation and repair.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by appropriate citations (Gupta et al. 2013) and the proteomic data showing KLH41 upregulation. C132 appropriately presents a speculative hypothesis about functional significance.

result: Absolute quantification using spiked-in peptides revealed RyR1 tetrameric complex content of 0.32 μmol/kg in WT EDL, with soleus and EOM containing 38% and 46% of EDL levels respectively. DHPRα1s content was 0.56 μmol/kg in EDL, 2.5-fold higher than soleus (0.18) and EOM (0.21). RyR1 tetramer:DHPRα1s ratios were 0.571 (WT EDL), 0.429 (dHT EDL), 0.667 (WT soleus), 0.625 (dHT soleus), 0.714 (WT EOM), and 0.474 (dHT EOM).
evaluation: Claims C134-C142 are supported by quantitative proteomic data in Tables 4-5 and Figure 5 (R²=0.96 calibration curve). The values are consistent with previous literature using different methods (Bers and Stiffel 1993), validating the approach. The stoichiometry data provide novel quantitative insights.

result: Stac3 content was highest in EDL (0.62 μmol/kg), with soleus and EOM containing ~1/3 of this level. Stac3:Cacna1s ratios were 1.11 (EDL), 1.22 (soleus), and 1.67 (EOM), with no differences between WT and dHT. The molar Stac3 content is 2.5-10-fold lower than its Kd (2-10 μM) for DHPRα1s, indicating <50% fractional occupancy. STAC3 mutations in NAM further decrease binding affinity, disrupting EC coupling.
evaluation: Claims C143-C146, C158-C163 are supported by quantitative proteomic data and appropriate citations (Rufenach et al. 2020; Polster et al. 2018; Wong King Yuen et al. 2017; Horstick et al. 2013). The fractional occupancy calculation is valid and provides important mechanistic insights into STAC3 function and disease.

result: EOMs contained the highest Stim1 levels (1.35 μmol/kg), ~3-fold higher than soleus (0.55) and EDL (0.46). Western blot confirmed EOMs have 4-fold more Stim1 than EDL, with equal Stim1:Stim1L ratios across muscles. Orai1 was highest in EOM (0.16 μmol/kg), with EDL at 68% of this level, but was undetectable in soleus. Stim1:Orai1 ratios were 23 (EDL) and 45 (EOM). The high Stim1/Orai1 in EOMs supports robust SOCE for continuous contraction.
evaluation: Claims C147-C157 are supported by quantitative proteomic data, Western blot validation (Figure 6), and appropriate citation (Cully et al. 2016). The absence of Orai1 in soleus raises important questions about SOCE mechanisms in slow-twitch muscle. C157 presents a reasonable interpretation.

result: Collagen VI mutations cause Ulrich/Bethlem myopathies with muscle contractures affecting elbows/ankles, a feature also seen in recessive RYR1 myopathies. Patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit skeletal abnormalities (scoliosis, hip dislocation, kyphosis, clubfoot, foot arch abnormalities) and joint laxity/contractures, which may relate to altered collagen composition observed in dHT mice.
evaluation: Claims C164-C168 are supported by appropriate citations (Bethlem and Wijngaarden 1976; Monnier et al. 2008; Klein et al. 2012; Jungbluth 2007). C169 appropriately presents a speculative connection between the proteomic findings and clinical features, though this requires further validation.

result: dHT muscles showed no upregulation of ER stress proteins (PERK, IRE1a, ATF6) but increased BiP and heat shock proteins in EDL/EOM. Small HSPs maintain cytoskeletal/contractile elements and aid myogenic differentiation. HSP levels increase with training but decrease with age. Multiple muscle diseases show HSP upregulation. Soleus showed no HSP upregulation, possibly due to constitutively 5-fold higher HSP70 levels, which may protect slow-twitch fibers and explain type 1 fiber predominance in RYR1 myopathies.
evaluation: Claims C170-C183 are supported by proteomic data and appropriate citations (Dreiza et al. 2010; Maglara et al. 2003; Martin et al. 1997; Murlasits et al. 2006; Vasilaki et al. 2002; Murgia et al. 2017; Brinkmeier and Ohlendieck 2014). C178 and C181 appropriately present interpretations/hypotheses. The HSP findings provide important mechanistic insights into differential muscle vulnerability.

result: Fast-twitch muscles appear first in development, are more severely affected in congenital myopathies, and undergo more prominent age-related atrophy. Patients with recessive RYR1 mutations are more severely affected, present from birth, and have widespread muscle weakness including facial and EOM involvement. Muscles from RYR1 mutation patients show type 1 fiber predominance.
evaluation: Claims C12-C14, C33-C35, C49, C90 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Lieber 2010; Schiaffino and Reggiani 2011; Buckingham et al. 2003; Jungbluth et al. 2005; Lawal et al. 2018; Nilwik et al. 2013; Amburgey et al. 2013). These establish important clinical context for interpreting the proteomic findings.

result: The authors conclude that recessive RYR1 mutations cause broad changes in protein expression affecting multiple signaling pathways and biological processes beyond just RyR1 reduction, with differential effects across muscle types (fast-twitch and EOMs more affected than slow-twitch).
evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C133 represent reasonable summary interpretations of the comprehensive proteomic data presented throughout the manuscript. The differential muscle type effects are clearly demonstrated by the data.

result: The manuscript cites established functional roles for several proteins: FKBP12 stabilizes RyR1, Hspb6 protects against atrophy/ischemia/stress, HSPs protect against calcium dysregulation and ischemic injury, Mitsugumin 53 mediates membrane repair, and S100A1 binds and regulates RyR1.
evaluation: Claims C71, C89, C91, C92, C94, C124 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Brillantes et al. 1994; Dreiza et al. 2010; Maglara et al. 2003; Martin et al. 1997; Cai et al. 2009; Treves et al. 1997; Prosser et al. 2011). These provide important functional context for interpreting the proteomic changes.
